attempts.label: DANDI:000251

inputs.what: The paper's own deposit, version 1 (2025-04-09). DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5 holds the cued delay task single units (spike, lick and event times, mouse, ML position), which DANDI:000251 does not hold; the cued delay claims are tested on it (data elsewhere). FinalAverageArray.mat, the paper's per-neuron table, is used to pair each neuron's VR and cued delay units (link claim) and, for the 11 cued delay neurons the HDF5 file lacks, to give their cue responses from its 10 ms rates; Valid_S.mat gives the paper's flags of the neurons recorded in each task. Files are streamed into memory; their SHA-256 sums from the deposit's file list are in the helper. The deposit is in Mendeley Data, which the registry does not read, so the paper cannot be listed on it there.

attempts.entry_title: Multi-timescale reinforcement learning in dopamine neurons (Masset et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in this data: dopamine neurons discount reward exponentially with a spread of discount factors, the population decodes reward timing, one value function fits the ramps in virtual reality, and each neuron's discount factor correlates across the two tasks. The advantage over a single-discount decoder held at some delays only, and the mean ramp slope came out below the paper's. The Figure 1 simulations were not run, for lack of time. The cued delay recordings are not on DANDI and were tested on the paper's own deposit, which lacks 11 of its 78 recorded neurons. Several supplementary results were weaker than reported, and one did not reproduce.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Masset, Tano, Kim, Malik, Pouget and Uchida (2025) on dandiset 000251, which holds the VR task single units of Kim et al. (2020), and on the paper's own Mendeley deposit, which holds the cued delay task units the dandiset lacks. It fits the common value function model to the ramping of VTA dopamine neurons, fits exponential and hyperbolic discounting to cue responses, decodes reward timing from the population, and compares discount factors across the two tasks through the paper's per-neuron table.

outcomes.statement: In simulations of a linear maze, agents learning values with three discount factors (0.6, 0.9, 0.99) report reward timing independently of magnitude, the hyperbolic value of the cue, reward timing before convergence and the true value under noisy rewards more accurately than agents with one or two discount factors.
outcomes.source: Results, Advantages of multi-timescale RL, Tasks 1 to 4; Figure 1e-f; Extended Data Fig. 1
outcomes.quote: Our result shows that only multi-timescale systems can reliably report the hyperbolic value of the cue given a diversity of exponential ones
outcomes.notes: Not attempted in this run. The claim rests on simulations made by the paper's public code (github.com/pablotano8/multi_timescale_RL at 37f11c6), not on any recorded data. The run's five hours went to the 25 outcomes on recorded data (24 of the paper's claims and the added link check), whose notebooks take about 115 minutes of computing in one run. A later attempt can run the simulation code.
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's simulation code, github.com/pablotano8/multi_timescale_RL at commit 37f11c6 (Fig_2_c_d_e.py)

outcomes.statement: With a small degree of shared value across discounts, the three-discount agent keeps its accuracy, 82, 94, 92 and 93% in Tasks 1 to 4.
outcomes.source: Methods, Mixing in distributed RL models, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: the accuracy of the report of the agent with three discounts {0.6,0.9,0.99} is 82 ± 5% in Task 1, 94 ± 2% in Task 2, 92 ± 3% in Task 3 and 93 ± 3% in Task 4
outcomes.notes: The sharing parameter of the mixing model (Methods eq. 32-33) is lost from the text, and the modification is not in the simulation repository at 37f11c6 nor in the Mendeley scripts, as the claims file records. No value of the parameter has a basis in the paper, so the reported accuracies cannot be checked. The question is in the findings.
outcomes.where: Not deposited; the sharing modification of eq. 32-33 is not in github.com/pablotano8/multi_timescale_RL at commit 37f11c6, and its sharing parameter is lost from the text

outcomes.statement: In a branching MDP learned from three trajectories, a two-discount agent with discounts 0.6 and 0.99 reaches 94% correct, more than single-discount agents (77% with 0.6, 83% with 0.99).
outcomes.source: Methods, Myopic learning bias, branching task, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 2e
outcomes.quote: For the single-discount agent, we report the maximum performance over the agents with discounts [0.6,0.6] and [0.99,0.99], which achieve a performance of 77±2% and 83±1% respectively. For the multi-discount agent, we use the discounts [0.6,0.99], which achieves a performance of 94±1%
outcomes.notes: Not attempted in this run, for the reason given for fig1f-multi-timescale-advantage (a simulation, Fig_2_f_myopic_mdp.py at 37f11c6).
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's simulation code, github.com/pablotano8/multi_timescale_RL at commit 37f11c6 (Fig_2_f_myopic_mdp.py)

outcomes.statement: Myopic value estimates are more accurate near important events and far-sighted ones far from them, in a grid-world maze learned from two trajectories and in the auxiliary Q-values of a DQN trained on Lunar Lander.
outcomes.source: Methods, Myopic learning bias, grid world and auxiliary tasks; Extended Data Fig. 2h and 2l
outcomes.quote: Q-values computed using a myopic discount provide a more accurate representation of the future when the agent is close to the landing site (blue in Extended Data Fig. 2k), whereas the opposite holds when the agent is far from the landing site
outcomes.notes: Not attempted in this run, for the reason given for fig1f-multi-timescale-advantage. The Lunar Lander part trains 10 DQNs, which would not fit the time left in any case.
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's simulation code, github.com/pablotano8/multi_timescale_RL at commit 37f11c6 (Ext_Fig_3_myopic_bias_maze.py, Fig_2_g_train_lunar_multi_gamma.py, Fig_2_g_lunar_q_accuracy.py)

outcomes.statement: The units of DANDI:000251 (VR task) and of the Mendeley cued delay file can each be matched to one row of the paper's per-neuron table, FinalAverageArray.mat, whose rows hold each neuron's VR and cued delay recordings.
outcomes.source: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1, FinalAverageArray.mat and Valid_S.mat (code Olfaction_Figure_Revision.m and Tuning_Figures_Revision.m index both tasks by the table's row)
outcomes.notes: All 101 DANDI open-loop units and all 67 Mendeley cued delay units match one distinct row each of FinalAverageArray.mat, 0.00 to 0.32 spikes per trial apart, with the next best row 3.8 or more apart, and the matched rows carry the files' ML positions. The table has 78 cued delay rows (all flagged Valid.OdorNew); 11 have no unit in the Mendeley file (4 of mouse 3044, 4 of 3049, 1 each of 3050, 3053 and 3054; 5 at ML above 900 um). Every one of the 67 rows with a cued delay unit also has a DANDI VR unit; 66 of these pairs were recorded on the same day. All 101 matched VR rows are flagged Valid.VR (121 rows flagged). Matching also shows that the cued delay trials are aligned on the VSTIM_ON column, the odor onset.

outcomes.statement: Of 78 optogenetically identified VTA dopamine neurons recorded in the cued delay task, 50 pass the selection criteria.
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 2; Methods, Fitting neural activity in the cued delay task, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: We recorded optogenetically identified single dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (n = 78, see Methods). We focused our analysis on neurons (n = 50) who passed the selection criteria
outcomes.notes: The Mendeley spike file holds 67 cued delay units, outside 78 +- 7.8, and 43 of them pass M3 under the claim's seed (43, 43, 45, 44 and 43 over the five seeds), outside 50 +- 5 except at seed plus 2000. Exclusions 17 (held-out R2 at or below 0), 10 (mean cue response at or below 2 spikes/s), 3 both, and none at ML 900 um or more, against the paper's 17, 11 and 4. The recorded count is outside tolerance at every seed, so the outcome is the same under all five. The selection behaves as in the paper (43 of 67 and 50 of 78 are both 0.64), and the shortfall is accounted for by the 11 neurons the paper's table flags (Valid.OdorNew) that are not in the deposit (5 at ML above 900 um). The claims file allows those flags only as labels where they can be matched to deposited units, which the 11 are not, so they are not counted here. As a variant, with their cue responses taken from the table's 10 ms rates, 48 of 78 pass M3 (48 to 50 over the seeds). The criterion's primary reading, the dandiset's marking of identified neurons, cannot be applied, as DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay units and the Mendeley file has no identification flag; the deposited units are taken as the identified neurons, each being a row the paper flags.
deviations: Tested on the paper's Mendeley deposit, as DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings.
The units are taken as the identified dopamine neurons; the file has no identification flag, and the link shows each unit is a row the paper flags Valid.OdorNew.
Cue responses are computed from the spike times (0.1 to 0.4 s after VSTIM_ON); the code reads precomputed per-trial rates (CellValuesArray.mat).

Fits use scipy's bounded least squares (least_squares) with the code's start points and bounds, where the code uses MATLAB fit; half splits are disjoint, where the code's two halves share one trial (Olfaction_Script.m, FirstHalf and SecondHalf).

The 11 cued delay neurons the spike file lacks (rows of the paper's table flagged Valid.OdorNew) are shown only as a variant, their cue responses being the mean of the table's 10 ms rates from 0.1 to 0.4 s after odor onset; on the 67 linked units these match the spike counts (mean absolute difference 0.43 spikes/s per trial, median correlation 0.987). The outcome does not use them.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Mice performed 81.4 +- 12.5 trials per session across 36 cued delay sessions and 58.8 +- 21.7 trials per session across 60 VR sessions with recorded neurons.
outcomes.source: Methods, Cued delay task, paragraph 2; Methods, Approach-to-target virtual reality task, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Mice performed 81.4 ± 12.5 trials (mean ± s.d.) per session across the 36 sessions in which neurons were recorded in the task ... Mice performed 58.8 ± 21.7 trials (mean ± s.d.) per session across the 60 sessions in which neurons were recorded in the task
outcomes.notes: On the deposited files, reading (a), every session with a unit, gives 39 cued delay sessions with 81.4 +- 12.7 trials and 66 VR sessions with 58.8 +- 19.5 trials, all within tolerance, with no random draws. The VR count sits on the upper bound of 60 +- 6. Reading (b), sessions with a unit of the analysed set, gives 62 VR sessions (59.2 trials) and 30 cued delay sessions (82.6 trials), the latter outside. The cued delay pass is weak evidence that the paper's count was reproduced, as it depends on the deposit being incomplete. The deposit lacks 11 of the 78 neurons the paper's table flags, and adding units can only add sessions; with them, as a variant, the table puts the 78 neurons in 44 sessions (reading a, 81.9 trials), outside tolerance, and 32 under reading (b) at the claim's seed (32 to 34 over the seeds). The VR units are those of the SU-VR-OL files, so the 78 units deposited twice are counted once. The VR files hold only the open-loop trials of the standard track and the cued delay file only the four odor trial types, so the two trial readings give the same counts. Sessions are a mouse and a start time, or for the table a mouse and session number (39 either way for the deposited units).
deviations: The cued delay half of the claim is tested on the Mendeley deposit (data with_inputs).
The 11 cued delay neurons the spike file lacks (rows of the paper's table flagged Valid.OdorNew) are shown only as a variant, from the table's 10 ms rates. The outcome does not use them.

outcomes.statement: Mice lick in anticipation of reward, and the onset of anticipatory licking is later for cues predicting longer delays.
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 2b
outcomes.quote: Importantly, the onset of the anticipatory licking was delayed for trials with cues predicting longer reward delays, indicating that the mice learned the delay contingencies
outcomes.notes: Under onset reading (a) the onset is at 0.3, 0.5, 2.3 and 7.9 s after the odor for the 0.6, 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s cues, over all 67 units and over the 43 selected, increasing with delay. Reading (b) (2 s.d. above the pre-cue bins) gives no order, as pre-cue licking is near zero (0.10 licks/s) and is crossed in the first bins. No random draws.
deviations: 67 units in place of the paper's 78 recorded neurons.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: The average cue response of the population decreases as the predicted reward delay increases.
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: the average responses to the reward cue decreased as the predicted reward timing increased
outcomes.notes: Over the 43 selected neurons the population mean falls monotonically, 11.68, 8.63, 3.70 and 2.86 spikes/s in 0.1 to 0.4 s and 8.77, 6.72, 3.30 and 2.71 in 0 to 0.5 s. It falls monotonically under all five seeds (43 to 45 neurons) and over all 67 units. With the 11 table neurons (48 selected) the means are 11.84, 8.86, 3.69 and 2.97 spikes/s, also decreasing.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Across neurons, the exponential discount model fits held-out cue responses better than the hyperbolic model (P = 2.2 x 10-5).
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 2f; Extended Data Fig. 3c-e
outcomes.quote: The exponential model provided a better fit to the neurons’ responses than the hyperbolic model (P = 2.2 x 10−5, two-tailed t-test, comparing the distribution across neurons of the mean (across bootstraps) difference in R2 between the two fits
outcomes.notes: Mean held-out R2 difference 0.0197 (exponential 0.456, hyperbolic 0.436), 34 of 43 neurons favour the exponential, t = 4.78, p = 2.2e-5 (paper 2.2 x 10-5). Over the five seeds p = 1.5e-5 to 4.6e-5. With the 11 table neurons (48 selected), mean difference 0.0208, p = 4.1e-6. A half-fit whose held-out responses are all equal has no R2 and is left out of the neuron's mean (20 to 29 of 13,400 half-fits per seed).
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Inferred discount factors are widely distributed across neurons, 0.56 +- 0.21 (mean +- s.d.).
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 2g
outcomes.quote: This view is consistent with the wide distribution of inferred discount factors obtained across the population (0.56 ± 0.21 s−1, mean ± s.d., Fig. 2g)
outcomes.notes: Mean 0.532 and s.d. 0.227 over 43 neurons under the claim's seed; over the five seeds the mean is 0.532 to 0.538 and the s.d. 0.223 to 0.227, all within tolerance. Mouse 3054 (19 neurons) has a mean of 0.658, mouse 3044 (16) 0.454, the other mice (8) 0.386. With the 11 table neurons (48 to 50 selected) the mean is 0.535 to 0.541 and the s.d. 0.214 to 0.217 over the seeds, also within tolerance.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Exponential-model parameters are consistent between the two halves of the trials; the mean correlation across neurons between halves is 0.84 for the gain, 0.9 for the baseline and 0.93 for the discount factor.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 3f
outcomes.quote: Distribution of correlations for the gain (mean = 0.84, P < 1 x 10−20), baseline b (v, mean = 0.9, P < 1.0 x 10−32) and discount factor (vi, mean = 0.93, P < 1.0 x 10−46)

statistics.test: Pearson correlation, highest p over bootstraps
Pearson correlation, highest p over bootstraps
Pearson correlation, highest p over bootstraps

outcomes.notes: Reading (a), the 43 selected neurons, gives mean split-half correlations of 0.735 (gain), 0.877 (baseline) and 0.815 (discount factor); reading (b), all 67 units, 0.555, 0.876 and 0.759. With the 11 table neurons added, 0.749, 0.884 and 0.796 (48 selected) and 0.570, 0.880 and 0.755 (all 78). The baseline is within tolerance, the gain and the discount factor are below it under every reading and all five seeds (gain 0.671 to 0.752, discount factor 0.717 to 0.817 under reading a). All correlations are positive and significant in every bootstrap (largest p 0.017). The parameters agree between halves, less closely than reported; the criterion has no partial clause, and partially reproduced is the protocol's case of an effect present but weaker.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Reward timing can be decoded from the population cue responses with a regularised inverse of the discount matrix, and decoding is better than with neuron identities shuffled (P = 1.2 x 10-4 at 0.6 s, P < 10-20 for the other delays).
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 2k; Extended Data Fig. 4f-g
outcomes.quote: Remarkably, the decoder was able to predict reward timing, closely matching the true reward delay (Fig. 2k, top row). This prediction was lost if we shuffled the neuron identities

statistics.about: 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s delays, data against shuffle

outcomes.notes: Under every reading (all components or the first 12; the Methods' or the code's baseline) and all five seeds, data beat shuffle at all four delays (largest p 0.012, at 0.6 s under seed plus 2000), and in all 20 shuffle draws. The two component readings give the same data decodings (largest difference 1.9e-6 s), as the singular components past the first few are too small to matter. Claim's seed, all components and the Methods' baseline, median distances 0.40, 0.84, 2.48 and 3.55 s against 1.15, 1.93, 3.45 and 7.13 s for the shuffle; p = 1.2e-11, 1.1e-34, 4.0e-18 and 8.5e-32.
deviations: The Wasserstein distance to the true delay is computed exactly (expected absolute distance); the code samples 100,000 points.
The number of singular components is open (DecodeTime is not in the deposit); both readings of the criterion are run and give the same outcome.
The shuffle control draws one permutation of the neurons per decoding, as the code; every reading uses the same permutations, and 20 draws are made, the first being the test.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Decoding with each neuron's own discount factor is more accurate than a single-discount model for the 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s delays, but not for 0.6 s.
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 2k bottom row; Extended Data Fig. 4e
outcomes.quote: Predictions from the model were more accurate than an alternative model with a single discount factor in which the response of each neuron is interpreted as a sample from the reward timing distribution
outcomes.notes: The population decoder is closer than the single-discount decoder at 1.5 s (p = 3.9e-32) and 9.375 s (p = 7.1e-25) but not at 3.75 s (p = 1; medians 2.48 against 1.89 s), under every reading and all five seeds (3.75 s p at least 0.997). At 0.6 s p = 0.69 (0.18 to 1 over seeds), no advantage, as in the paper. Two of the three delays the criterion names.
outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.statement: Decoding with the exponential discount matrix is more accurate than with the hyperbolic one for the 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s delays.
outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 6d-e
outcomes.quote: the accuracy of reward timing decoding was typically higher when using the discount matrix from the exponential model than the one from the hyperbolic model
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' baseline the exponential matrix is better at 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s under all five seeds (p at most 1.1e-8) and not at 0.6 s. With the code's baseline the 9.375 s result varies with the seed (p = 0.0095 under the claim's seed, 0.98 under seed plus 2000), so the outcome rests on the Methods' baseline, which the claims file names as the main reading. outcomes.where: Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1 (version 1), file DA_SU_ODOR_NEW_W_OL.h5, the paper's own deposit; DANDI:000251 holds no cued delay recordings

outcomes.source: Results, Discounting across dopamine neurons, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 6f-g

outcomes.statement: In the VR task, 90 dopamine neurons ramp up on average before reward (mean slope 0.097, P = 0.0175), but single neurons vary, 53 with significant positive slopes, 32 with significant negative slopes and 5 not significant.
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 2; Figure 3b
outcomes.quote: the slope of the activity ramp (computed between the two black horizontal ticks in main panel) is positive on average but varies across neurons (population: mean slope = 0.097, P = 0.0175. Single neurons: positive and P < 0.05: n = 53; negative and P < 0.05: n = 32; P > 0.05: n = 5, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: 91 neurons pass M6 (31 of mouse 3044, 23 of 3054, 37 of eight other mice). Mean slope 0.084 (p = 0.018), below 0.097 +- 0.0097; 51 positive, 34 negative and 6 non-significant slopes. The population slope is positive and significant and the neuron count within tolerance, while the non-significant count (and the mean slope) are not, which is the criterion's partial case. The same under all five seeds (mean slope 0.0833 to 0.0837, counts unchanged). The window's last bin reaches a median 0.042 s past the reward (95th percentile 0.078 s); with the z-score s.d. over bins 1 to 42 only, the mean slope is 0.0849 (p = 0.017) and the counts the same.
deviations: PSTHs are spike counts in 43 bins of 0.1 s from 3.05 to 7.35 s after scene motion onset (Methods); the code averages 10 ms rates in 43 bins that share their edge samples, ending at the reward time of its table.
Half splits are disjoint; the code's halves share one trial.

outcomes.statement: A model with one convex value function shared across neurons and a discount factor, gain and baseline per neuron captures the diversity of ramping, with discount factors distributed as 0.42 +- 0.23 (mean +- s.d.).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Figure 3e, 3f, 3k and 3l
outcomes.quote: The heterogeneity of ramping activity across single neurons is explained (Fig. 3e,f) by a common convex value function (Fig. 3k) and a diversity of discount factors across single neurons (Fig. 3l)
outcomes.notes: Mean 0.446 and s.d. 0.237 of the per-neuron discount factors under the claims' seeds (0.437 to 0.447 and 0.231 to 0.243 over the five), within tolerance. The mean value function is convex under both readings (second difference positive at 66 to 68% of bins; at or below the chord at every interior bin). Percentiles 20, 70 and 90 are 0.220, 0.555 and 0.731 (paper 0.25, 0.56, 0.88). Few fits reach the optimiser's tolerance (9 to 16 of 200 per seed). On 20 fits the iteration cap moves the mean from 0.479 (3000 iterations) to 0.443 (10,000) and 0.442 (30,000). All 200 fits of the claims' seed at 30,000 iterations give mean 0.442 and s.d. 0.238 (96 of 200 reach the tolerance), also within tolerance.
deviations: Assumption. The fit is capped at 10,000 iterations of L-BFGS-B, with gains and baselines solved exactly at each step (variable projection, same bounds), where the code runs fmincon (interior point, MaxIter 2000, TolFun 1e-5). The cap is chosen because 30,000 iterations change the result little on a subset while 3000 change it; the paper does not say how far its fits converged.

outcomes.statement: The inferred VR discount factor and the ramp slope are strongly correlated (r = 0.81).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 8b
outcomes.quote: The inferred discount factor and the slope in spiking activity (see Fig. 3b) are strongly correlated (r = 0.81, P = 0, Spearman rank correlation, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: Spearman r = 0.709 (p = 3.6e-15, 91 neurons) under the claims' seeds, below 0.81 +- 0.081. Over the five seeds r = 0.708 to 0.753; under seeds plus 2000 (0.753) and plus 3000 (0.744) it is within tolerance. On 20 fits r rises with the iteration cap (0.618 at 3000, 0.718 at 10,000, 0.732 at 30,000), so the value depends on how far the fits converge. All 200 fits of the claims' seed at 30,000 iterations give r = 0.726 (p = 3.8e-16), still below 0.729.
deviations: Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: The VR discount factor is not correlated with the medio-lateral position of the implant (r = 0.015, P = 0.89).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 7c
outcomes.quote: The discount factor inferred in the VR task is not correlated with the medio-lateral (ML) position of the implant (Pearson’s r = 0.015, P = 0.89, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: Pearson r = -0.031, p = 0.77 (paper r = 0.015, P = 0.89); over the five seeds r = -0.038 to -0.027, p at least 0.72. The 91 neurons come from 10 implants, with 10 distinct ML values (320 to 846 um).
deviations: Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: Discount factors from the common value model and the common reward expectation model are strongly correlated across neurons (rho = 0.93).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9g
outcomes.quote: the inferred discount factors are strongly correlated for single neurons (Spearman’s ρ = 0.93, P < 1.0 x 10−20, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: Spearman rho = 0.743 (p = 3.3e-17, 91 neurons) between the per-neuron mean discount factors of the two models over 200 fits each under the claims' seeds, below 0.93 +- 0.093. 187 of the 200 reward expectation fits converged, and the constraint holds in all to within 1.1e-6. Under the four other seeds, on the first 10 bootstraps (20 fits), rho = 0.769 to 0.809, also below. The discount factors are strongly correlated, less than reported. The reward expectation model puts 17 neurons below 0.06, at the lower bound of 0.05 (its mean discount factor 0.218, against 0.446 for the common value model).
deviations: The reward expectation model is fitted by SLSQP with analytic gradients (checked against finite differences), at most 2000 iterations, where the code uses fmincon (interior point); the optimiser is a substitute.
The folded normal density is written as a sum of two Gaussians, equal to the code's FoldedNormal.m, which overflows at small widths (the code sets the resulting values to 1e-4).
Under the four other seeds only the first 10 bootstraps are fitted (20 fits), for time.
Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: For the 43 neurons recorded in both tasks, the discount factors inferred in the VR task and the cued delay task are correlated (Spearman r = 0.45, P = 0.0013).
outcomes.source: Results, Correlated discount factors across tasks, paragraph 2; Figure 4a
outcomes.quote: Correlation across neurons between the discount factors inferred in the VR task and the discount factors inferred in the cued delay task (r = 0.45, P = 0.0013, Spearman’s rank correlation, one-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: 40 neurons pass both selections (16 of m3044, 18 of m3054, 4 of m3045, 2 of m3053); Spearman r = 0.462, one-tailed p = 0.0013 (paper 0.45, 0.0013). Over the five cued delay seeds 40 to 42 neurons, r = 0.461 to 0.471. The 39 pairs recorded on the same day give r = 0.439 (p = 0.0026). The VR fit is the one at the claims' seeds.
deviations: Neurons are paired through the paper's per-neuron table (link-units-across-tasks).
Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: Correlations between the two tasks' discount factors over random pairs of bootstrap estimates are positive, 0.34 +- 0.104 (mean +- s.d.).
outcomes.source: Figure 4b
outcomes.quote: Distribution of Spearman’s rank correlation correlations between the discount factors across the two tasks for randomly sampled pairs of bootstrap estimates (0.34 ± 0.104, mean ± s.d., P < 1.0 x 10−30, one-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), the code's draw from the first halves, gives mean 0.364 and s.d. 0.104 under the claim's seed (10,000 pairs); reading (b), all 200 half-fits, 0.342 and 0.107. Both are within tolerance; p is printed as 0. Under seed plus 3000 neither reading has the s.d. within tolerance (0.115 and 0.116 against 0.104 +- 0.0104); under the other seeds at least one reading does. 100,000 pairs give the same values.
deviations: Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: Reward timing in the cued delay task can be decoded with the discount factors inferred in the VR task, better than shuffle for the 1.5, 3.75 and 9.375 s delays.
outcomes.source: Results, Correlated discount factors across tasks, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 10c-d
outcomes.quote: we were able to decode subjective reward timing from population cue responses using the discount matrix built from the discount factors inferred in the virtual reality task
outcomes.notes: Data beat shuffle at 1.5 and 3.75 s under every reading, seed and shuffle draw (p at most 2.9e-15 under the claim's seed), but under the claim's seed not at 9.375 s: p = 0.098 with the Methods' baseline (6 of 20 draws below 0.05, median p 0.10) and 0.83 with the code's (none of 20). At 0.6 s p is at least 0.996, as in the paper. Under seed plus 2000, 9.375 s passes (p = 0.0079 and 0.0023 for the two baselines; 13 and 17 of 20 draws), which would make the claim reproduced; under plus 1000, 3000 and 4000 it does not (first-draw p 0.15 to 0.93, at most 3 of 20 draws). The two component readings give the same result.
deviations: The test responses are shuffled, as M4 says; the code (Tuning_Figures_Revision.m) shuffles the training responses.
The shuffle control draws one permutation of the neurons per decoding, as the code; every reading uses the same permutations, and 20 draws are made, the first being the test.
Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: The VR baseline and gain are not significantly correlated with the medio-lateral position of the implant (baseline r = -0.011, P = 0.92; gain r = -0.19, P = 0.069).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 7d-e
outcomes.quote: The baseline parameter inferred in the VR task is not correlated with the medio-lateral (ML) position of the implant (Pearson’s r = −0.011, P = 0.92, two-tailed t-test). e, The inferred gain in the VR task reduces with increasing medio-lateral (ML) position but the effect does not reach significance (Pearson’s r = −0.19, P = 0.069, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: Baseline r = 0.026 (p = 0.81), gain r = -0.175 (p = 0.097) under the claims' seeds (paper -0.011 and -0.19); over the five seeds the gain's p is 0.093 to 0.104, the baseline's at least 0.77. The gain is the code's stored a / gamma^0.1.
deviations: Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: In the VR task, the ramp in anticipatory licking is not correlated with the neural discount factor in either of the two mice with most neurons, whichever pair of the three lick windows measures the ramp.
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 8c-d
outcomes.quote: the neural discount factor and the ramp in licking activity is not correlated irrespective of the window used to compute the ramp in licking activity
outcomes.notes: With the Methods windows (before each trial's reward) none of the six correlations has p < 0.05 under any seed (smallest 0.315, m3044 middle against early); under the claims' seeds r ranges from -0.064 to 0.173. The code's windows (aligned on scene motion) give the same under the claims' seeds (smallest p 0.27). Neurons are the M6 neurons of each mouse (31 and 23).
deviations: Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

outcomes.statement: Fitted to the neurons of one mouse alone (m3044, 29 neurons; m3054, 24 neurons), the common value model gives gains, baselines and discount factors strongly correlated with those of the full population fit (discount factor r = 0.75 in m3044 and 0.88 in m3054).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping heterogeneity and discounting, paragraph 4; Methods, Common Value Function model, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 8e-j
outcomes.quote: Furthermore, the model fit was robust when applied at the single animal level for the two animals with sufficient numbers of neurons
outcomes.notes: Under the claim's seed five of the six r are within tolerance, and the m3044 gain (0.700) is just below 0.702; all p < 1e-4. The code compares the population's stored gain a / gamma^0.1 with the per-mouse fit's a (Master_Script_SingleValue_All_gain.m lines 429 to 431, Master_Script_SingleValue_m3044.m lines 435 to 437, VR_Figures_Revision.m lines 909 and 1051); the like-for-like gains give 0.698 (a against a) and 0.674 (a / gamma^0.1 on both sides) in m3044, also below, and 0.968 and 0.966 in m3054, so the gain reading does not change the outcome. Under the other four seeds all six are within tolerance with the code's comparison (m3044 gain 0.703 to 0.759), which would make the claim reproduced. Neuron counts 31 (29 +- 2.9) and 23 (24 +- 2.4).
deviations: Each mouse is fitted with new splits and initial values, as the code's per-mouse scripts do, and compared with the population fit at the claims' seeds.
The like-for-like gain comparisons are shown as variants; the test is the code's, which the criterion cites.
Rests on the iteration cap of the common value fit (see fig3-common-value-fit).

findings.statement: 78 open-loop units are deposited twice. Each SU-VR-ALL-OL file holds the same spike train as an SU-VR-OL file of the same subject, under another session number (for example sub-3014 SU-VR-ALL-OL-1 and SU-VR-OL-2). The two files of each pair have different identifiers and session IDs and the same generic session description ("Data for Kim et al. 2020."); they share the subject and session start time, as do files that hold different units of one session (59 of 165 subject and start time pairs hold more than one distinct spike train), and the dandiset's description does not mention the copies. An analysis of all single-unit files counts these units twice.
findings.checked: The outputs show it, in vr_population cell 4: "257 distinct spike trains in 336 files; 78 deposited more than once". All 78 SU-VR-ALL-OL files share a spike train with an SU-VR-OL file under another session number, 77 pairs plus one group that also includes SU-VR-ALL-TP-3; the match is on an exact hash of the spike times. Not shown is that nothing in the files says so; session IDs, start times and descriptions of the pairs are not compared. critical is right; a unit deposited as two with nothing linking the copies is the defining case, and counting all single-unit files double-counts 78 units.

findings.statement: sub-3015/sub-3015_ses-SU-VR-OL-4.nwb, named as an open-loop session, holds a teleport session; its trial table has the four teleport trial types, and its spike train is the same as that of SU-VR-ALL-TP-3 and SU-VR-ALL-OL-3.

The dandiset holds no cued delay (odor) task recordings, although the paper's deposit (doi:10.17632/tc43t3s7c5.1) says its raw electrophysiological data are in DANDI:000251. Only the VR task single units are there; the cued delay units are in the Mendeley deposit.

The single-unit files have no description of their units and no flag for optogenetic identification, and the dandiset's description does not say which units are identified dopamine neurons. The paper's own flags (Valid_S.mat in its Mendeley deposit) mark all 101 open-loop units as analysed, so the units can be taken as identified only through that deposit.
The dandiset has no published version; it exists only as a draft (last modified 2023-06-20), which can change and has no DOI.

Checks that passed. All 101 open-loop units match the paper's per-neuron table trial by trial, and the spikes, licks and trial events share one clock (reward responses at the trial table's reward times, none at times shifted by 5 s). The reward comes a median 7.31 s after scene motion onset in the files, where the paper gives 7.35 s.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebooks (vr_population, vr_single_mouse, cued_delay_and_cross_task) with the conclusion cells and the summaries removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's full text. The verifier read the archive's metadata and tested helpers on synthetic inputs (_ab_given, wasserstein_to_point, fit_exp, the analytic gradient of cv_sse, the decoder's filter). It had no attempt record.

disagreements.reason: Valid.OdorNew flags 78 rows, matching 78 (the criterion's variant). The Mendeley file holds only 67 units, and 43 are selected at the claim seed (45 at one other seed), outside 50 +- 5. Six of the 11 flagged units missing from the file have ML <900 um, so part of the shortfall is missing data. Bounds on the selected count with them (at most 49) would settle the claim.
Gain 0.735 and gamma 0.815 (selected set), or 0.555 and 0.76 (all units), are below the tolerances (at least 0.756 and 0.837). Only the baseline (0.877) passes (cell 22).
r = 0.709 at the claim seed, below 0.729. Two of five seeds fall inside (0.755, 0.740) (cell 18).

Reproduced, but fragile. At the claim seed, reading (a) with the Methods baseline gives p = 0.014 at 9.375 s. The same decoder with a different shuffle draw gives p = 0.16, and 9.375 s passes in only 5 of 10 Methods-baseline runs (cell 41). 1.5 and 3.75 s are robust.

verifications.reviewed: The executed notebooks of the round-1 revision (vr_population, vr_single_mouse, vr_reward_expectation, cued_delay_and_cross_task) with their conclusions and summaries, the attempt record, the README, the claims file and its own round-1 report, with the paper's full text.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: Round 3. The two proposed changes of outcome, on cued-delay-neurons and session-trial-counts, with the analysis behind them in the printed outputs of cued_delay_and_cross_task.ipynb (cells 3, 6, 8, 13 and 48), the attempt record and the claims file. Nothing else was reviewed. The verifier agreed with both proposals. It also noted three places where the claims file does not fit the data, none of them a misreading of the paper. Report in transcripts/masset-2025/verifier-3-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The paper's Mendeley deposit holds 67 of the 78 cued delay units of its own table (Valid.OdorNew); 11 are missing, 5 of them at ML above 900 um. Its HDF5 file does not say that the VSTIM_ON event column is the odor onset (the alignment of the paper's table and the reward times show that it is).

Question for the authors. How far did the common value model fits converge? The code caps fmincon at 2000 iterations; here few fits reach a tolerance even at 10,000 L-BFGS-B iterations, and the population's discount factors and their correlation with the ramp slope change with the cap (on 20 fits, mean 0.479 at 3000 iterations, 0.443 at 10,000; Spearman with the slope 0.62 and 0.72). This attempt assumes 10,000 iterations.

Question for the authors. DecodeTime, the decoder of Fig. 2k, is not in the deposit. Does it use every singular component of the discount matrix (Eq. 21-22) or the first 12, as the single-discount SVD in the code does? Both were run here and give the same outcomes.

Question for the authors. The sharing parameter of the mixing model (Methods, Mixing in distributed RL models) is lost from the text, and the code that adds sharing to the agents is in neither deposit. What value gives the reported 82, 94, 92 and 93% accuracies?

The Methods exclude 17 neurons for negative held-out R2, 11 for a low cue response and 4 for ML above 900 um from 78, which leaves 46, not the 50 analysed; Extended Data Fig. 3b shows 23 non-selected neurons and Fig. 3c 13 with negative R2. On the deposited units this attempt finds 17, 10 (3 overlapping) and 0. With the 11 neurons the spike file lacks taken from the paper's table, the counts are 18, 11 and 5, and 48 neurons pass.

The code's half splits (Olfaction_Script.m and Master_Script_SingleValue_All_gain.m, PermutedOrder(1 to floor(n/2)) and PermutedOrder(ceil(n/2) to n)) give two halves that share one trial, where the Methods describe a split of the trials in halves. This attempt uses disjoint halves.

VR_Figures_Revision.m (lines 909 and 1051) correlates the population fit's stored gain, a / gamma^0.1 (Master_Script_SingleValue_All_gain.m lines 429 to 431), with the per-mouse fit's a (Master_Script_SingleValue_m3044.m lines 435 to 437), and the per-mouse scripts call Cost_VR_SingleValue_Norm_All.m, which is not in the deposit. Here the like-for-like gains give about the same correlations.

entries.name: masset-2025
entries.title: Multi-timescale reinforcement learning in dopamine neurons (Masset et al. 2025)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Masset, Tano, Kim, Malik, Pouget and Uchida (2025) on dandiset 000251, which holds the VR task single units of Kim et al. (2020), and on the paper's own Mendeley deposit, which holds the cued delay task units the dandiset lacks. It fits the common value function model to the ramping of VTA dopamine neurons, fits exponential and hyperbolic discounting to cue responses, decodes reward timing from the population, and compares discount factors across the two tasks through the paper's per-neuron table.
